docs.title: Step 7: Run the migration (Replication clusters only)
docs.text:
Replication Migration — Primary/Replica clusters only

This step is only required forPrimary/Replica (replication)clusters. If you are running aGalera cluster, skip this step.

After the operator upgrade, you must run the replication migration script to reset and re-establish replication on each replica pod.

The script automatically identifies the primary pod (skips it) and processes only the replicas. For each replica it:

  • Runs STOP SLAVE and RESET SLAVE ALL via kubectl exec
  • Deletes the pod so it gets recreated
  • Waits for it to come back ready
  • Verifies replication is working again

Set the required environment variables: 

    export MARIADB_NAME=mariadb-cluster
    export MARIADB_NAMESPACE=openstack
    export MARIADB_ROOT_PASSWORD=$(kubectl get secret mariadb -n openstack \
      -o jsonpath='{.data.root-password}' | base64 -d)

Save the script to a file (e.g. /tmp/migrate-replication.sh):

migrate-replication.sh (click to expand)

migrate-replication.sh 

    #!/bin/bash

    set -eo pipefail

    if [[ -z "$MARIADB_NAME" || -z "$MARIADB_NAMESPACE" || -z "$MARIADB_ROOT_PASSWORD" ]]; then
      echo "Error: MARIADB_NAME, MARIADB_NAMESPACE and MARIADB_ROOT_PASSWORD env vars must be set."
      exit 1
    fi

    function exec_sql {
      local pod=$1
      local sql=$2
      kubectl exec -n "$MARIADB_NAMESPACE" "$pod" -- mariadb -u root -p"$MARIADB_ROOT_PASSWORD" -e "$sql"
    }

    function wait_for_ready_replication {
      local pod=$1
      local timeout=300  # 5 minutes
      local interval=10  # Check every 10 seconds
      local elapsed=0

      echo "Waiting for ready replication on $pod..."

      while [[ $elapsed -lt $timeout ]]; do
          local status
          status=$(exec_sql "$pod" "SHOW REPLICA STATUS\G" | tee /tmp/replication_status_$pod_$MARIADB_NAMESPACE.txt)

          if grep -q "Slave_IO_Running: Yes" /tmp/replication_status_$pod_$MARIADB_NAMESPACE.txt && \
             grep -q "Slave_SQL_Running: Yes" /tmp/replication_status_$pod_$MARIADB_NAMESPACE.txt; then
            echo "Replication is ready on $pod."
            return 0
          fi

          echo "Replication not ready on $pod. Retrying in $interval seconds..."
          sleep $interval
          ((elapsed+=interval))
      done

      echo "Error: Replication did not become ready on $pod within 5 minutes."
      exit 1
    }

    echo "Migrating replication on $MARIADB_NAME instance..."

    PODS=$(kubectl get pods -n "$MARIADB_NAMESPACE" \
      -l app.kubernetes.io/instance=$MARIADB_NAME \
      -o jsonpath="{.items[*].metadata.name}")
    PRIMARY_POD=$(kubectl get mariadb "$MARIADB_NAME" -n "$MARIADB_NAMESPACE" \
      -o jsonpath="{.status.currentPrimary}")

    for POD in $PODS; do
      if [[ "$POD" == "$PRIMARY_POD" ]]; then
          printf "\nSkipping primary pod: $POD\n"
          continue
      fi
      printf "\nProcessing replica pod: $POD\n"

      echo "Resetting replication on $POD..."
      exec_sql "$POD" "STOP SLAVE 'mariadb-operator';"
      exec_sql "$POD" "RESET SLAVE 'mariadb-operator' ALL;"

      echo "Deleting pod $POD..."
      kubectl delete pod "$POD" -n "$MARIADB_NAMESPACE"

      echo "Waiting for pod $POD to become ready..."
      kubectl wait --for=condition=Ready pod/"$POD" -n "$MARIADB_NAMESPACE" --timeout=5m
      echo "Pod $POD is ready."

      wait_for_ready_replication "$POD"
    done

    echo "Replication migration completed successfully on $MARIADB_NAME instance."

Make it executable and run: 

    chmod +x /tmp/migrate-replication.sh
    /tmp/migrate-replication.sh

Stuck replication threads

If stuck replication threads are observed, identify and kill them:

      -u root -p"$MARIADB_ROOT_PASSWORD" -e "SHOW PROCESSLIST;"

      -u root -p"$MARIADB_ROOT_PASSWORD" -e "KILL <thread_id>;"

    mariadb-operator/mariadb-operator       0.37.0          0.37.0      Run and operate MariaDB in a cloud native way

and you can directly jump from 0.38.1 → 25.8.4

Kubernetes version requirement

25.8.4 requires Kubernetes >= 1.34.

Known Issue: Webhook cert validation loop

If operator pods are stuck logging: 

    {"level":"info","ts":...,"logger":"setup","msg":"Validating certs"}

Check the certificate: 

    kubectl get certificate -n mariadb-system

If you see Existing private key is not up to date for spec: [spec.privateKey.algorithm], fix by deleting the secret and webhook deployment: 

    kubectl delete secret mariadb-operator-webhook-cert -n mariadb-system
    kubectl delete deployment mariadb-operator-webhook -n mariadb-system

Then re-run the install script to recreate them.

Skip 25.10.0, You do not need to step through each patch releases in between 25.8.x - using the above standard procedure.

Patch-by-patch upgrade is NOT required for 25.10.x

You do not need to step through each patch releases in between 25.8.x - using the above standard procedure: 

    25.10.1 → 25.10.2 → 25.10.3 → 25.10.4

For 25.10.4, Follow the standard procedure. No special steps required beyond the standard preflight and upgrade.

References

  • Release 26.3.0

Breaking Change: syncBinlog type change (Replication clusters)

syncBinlog changed from booleantointeger. This affects Primary/Replica (replication) clusters. Galera clusters without replication in their spec are not affected.

If the existing MariaDB CR has syncBinlog: true, the new webhook will reject patches. Remove the webhook before patching: 

    kubectl delete validatingwebhookconfiguration mariadb-operator-webhook
    kubectl -n openstack patch mariadb mariadb-cluster --type merge \
      -p '{"spec":{"replication":{"syncBinlog":1}}}'

Then re-run the install script to restore the webhook.

Breaking Change: Image configuration format

Image configuration in Helm values changed from string to structured format:

Old FormatNew Format 

    config:
      mariadbImageName: repo/image:tag_version

    config:
      mariadbImage:
        repository: repo/image
        tag: <version>

Ensure /etc/genestack/helm-configs/mariadb-operator/mariadb-operator-helm-overrides.yaml uses the new format for maxscaleImage, exporterImage, exporterMaxscaleImage image sections before upgrading to 26.3.0.

New CRD

A new CRD is added with this version: pointintimerecoveries.k8s.mariadb.com

docs.title: Webhook blocks patches due to old stored values
docs.text:
If the webhook rejects changes because the existing resource in etcd has old-format values (e.g. syncBinlog: true), temporarily remove the webhook: 

    kubectl scale deployment mariadb-operator -n mariadb-system --replicas=0
    kubectl scale deployment mariadb-operator-webhook -n mariadb-system --replicas=0
    kubectl delete validatingwebhookconfiguration mariadb-operator-webhook
    kubectl delete mutatingwebhookconfiguration mariadb-operator-webhook 2>/dev/null || true

Apply the fix, then re-run the install script to restore everything.

    kubectl delete deployment mariadb-operator-webhook -n mariadb-system
    /opt/genestack/bin/install-mariadb-operator.sh

docs.title: NVIDIA Multi-Instance GPU (MIG) for Inference
docs.text: MIG allows a single physical GPU to be partitioned into isolated instances, each with dedicated compute, memory, and cache resources. This is transformative for multi-tenant inference.

docs.title: Why MIG for Production Inference
docs.text:
• Hardware isolation — each MIG instance has dedicated SM (Streaming Multiprocessor) slices, memory bandwidth, and L2 cache
  • QoS guarantees — noisy neighbor problem eliminated; one model can't starve another
  • Cost efficiency — serve multiple small models on one H100 instead of dedicating an entire 80GB GPU to a 7B model using 14GB
  • Fault isolation — an OOM in one instance doesn't crash others

docs.text: Profile Memory Compute (SMs) Use Case 1g.10gb 10 GB 1/7 (16 SMs) 7B INT4/INT8 quantized models 2g.20gb 20 GB 2/7 (32 SMs) 7B FP16, small embedding models 3g.40gb 40 GB 3/7 (48 SMs) 13B FP16 or 70B AWQ/GPTQ 4g.40gb 40 GB 4/7 (64 SMs) 13B with large batch sizes 7g.80gb 80 GB 7/7 (132 SMs) 70B FP16, full GPU for one model

docs.title: MIG Configuration on OpenShift
docs.text:
apiVersion: nvidia.com/v1
kind: ClusterPolicy
metadata:
  name: gpu-cluster-policy
spec:
  operator:
    defaultRuntime: crio
  driver:
    enabled: true
  devicePlugin:
    enabled: true
  migManager:
    enabled: true
    config:
      name: mig-config
  dcgmExporter:
    enabled: true
  gfd:
    enabled: true
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: mig-config
  namespace: nvidia-gpu-operator
data:
  config.yaml: |
    version: v1
    mig-configs:
      # Inference-optimized: 2× large + 4× small instances per GPU
      inference-mixed:
        - devices: [0, 1]
          mig-enabled: true
          mig-devices:
            "3g.40gb": 2    # Two 40GB slices → 13B models each
        - devices: [2, 3]
          mig-enabled: true
          mig-devices:
            "1g.10gb": 7    # Seven 10GB slices → 7B quantized models
        - devices: [4, 5, 6, 7]
          mig-enabled: false  # Full GPUs for TP across 4 GPUs (70B model)

      # Training: all GPUs full (no MIG)
      training-full:
        - devices: all
          mig-enabled: false

      # Multi-tenant small models
      multi-tenant-small:
        - devices: all
          mig-enabled: true
          mig-devices:
            "2g.20gb": 3    # Three 20GB slices per GPU = 24 instances on 8 GPUs

│ GPU 0-1: MIG 3g.40gb × 2 each = 4 instances                    │
│   → 4× 13B model replicas (one per MIG instance)               │

docs.title: NCCL Tuning for Multi-GPU Communication
docs.text:
env:
  # Use InfiniBand for NCCL (multi-node training)
  - name: NCCL_IB_DISABLE
    value: "0"
  - name: NCCL_IB_HCA
    value: "mlx5_0,mlx5_1,mlx5_2,mlx5_3"
  - name: NCCL_IB_GID_INDEX
    value: "3"
  # Use NVLink for intra-node (tensor parallelism)
  - name: NCCL_P2P_LEVEL
    value: "NVL"           # Force NVLink for peer-to-peer
  - name: NCCL_NET_GDR_LEVEL
    value: "PIX"           # GPU Direct RDMA level
  # Buffering and threading
  - name: NCCL_BUFFSIZE
    value: "8388608"       # 8MB buffers (default 4MB)
  - name: NCCL_NTHREADS
    value: "512"           # Max threads per NCCL operation
  - name: NCCL_SOCKET_IFNAME
    value: "eth2"          # GPU fabric interface
  # Topology detection
  - name: NCCL_TOPO_DUMP_FILE
    value: "/tmp/nccl_topo.xml"

docs.text:
If using RoCEv2 instead of InfiniBand:

# Enable Priority Flow Control (PFC) on switch ports
# (switch-specific — example for Mellanox/NVIDIA Spectrum)
interface ethernet 1/1-1/32
  dcb priority-flow-control mode on
  dcb priority-flow-control priority 3 enable
  dcb ets traffic-class 3 bandwidth 80

# Enable ECN on the host

mlnx_qos -i eth2 --pfc 0,0,0,1,0,0,0,0    # PFC on priority 3
cma_roce_tos -d mlx5_0 -t 106               # DSCP for RoCE traffic

docs.title: Model Loading Strategy
docs.text:
Models are large (7B = 14GB, 70B = 140GB FP16). Loading speed directly impacts pod startup time and autoscaler responsiveness.

┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  Model Loading Pipeline                                       │
│                                                               │
│  S3 (source of truth)  ──→  CephFS (shared warm cache)       │
│         │                          │                          │
│         │  (first pull)            │  (fast local cache)      │
│         ▼                          ▼                          │
│  ┌─────────────┐          ┌─────────────────────┐            │
│  │  Init Container│        │  hostPath NVMe       │            │
│  │  (model pull)  │──────→│  /mnt/model-cache    │            │
│  └─────────────┘          └──────────┬──────────┘            │
│                                       │                       │
│                                       ▼                       │
│                            ┌─────────────────────┐            │
│                            │  vLLM loads from     │            │
│                            │  local NVMe (6GB/s)  │            │
│                            └─────────────────────┘            │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
Storage Path Load Time (140GB model) S3 over 25GbE ~56 seconds CephFS over 100GbE ~14 seconds Local NVMe (pre-cached) ~20 seconds

docs.text:
apiVersion: monitoring.coreos.com/v1
kind: PrometheusRule
metadata:
  name: vllm-performance-alerts
  namespace: model-serving
spec:
  groups:
    - name: vllm-throughput
      rules:
        - alert: VLLMHighQueueDepth
          expr: avg(vllm_num_requests_waiting) > 20
          for: 2m
          labels:
            severity: warning
          annotations:
            summary: "vLLM request queue backing up"
            description: "Average queue depth {{ $value }} — consider scaling up"

        - alert: VLLMKVCacheSaturation
          expr: avg(vllm_gpu_cache_usage_perc) > 90
          for: 1m
          labels:
            severity: critical
          annotations:
            summary: "KV cache near saturation — requests will be preempted"

        - alert: GPUThermalThrottle
          expr: DCGM_FI_DEV_GPU_TEMP > 83
          for: 30s
          labels:
            severity: critical
          annotations:

docs.text: An interactive, animated architecture diagram for Red Hat OpenStack Services on OpenShift (RHOSO) 18.0, built with FlowStory. A single self-contained HTML file that visualizes 38 operational flows with 632 animated steps across the podified control plane, EDPM data plane, and external storage.

docs.title: What Is This?
docs.text:
RHOSO 18.0 runs the OpenStack control plane as Kubernetes-native pods on Red Hat OpenShift, while managing bare-metal compute nodes via the External Data Plane Management (EDPM) pattern. Understanding how requests traverse these boundaries — from API call to VM boot to OVN packet path — is non-trivial.

This visualizer makes it concrete. Each flow animates step-by-step through the real components, showing API payloads in the inspector panel and letting you click any node for a detailed tooltip.

docs.title: How It Was Built
docs.text:
The visualizer is a single flow.html file using the FlowStory framework:

  • CSS loaded from noyitz.github.io/flowstory/templates/style.css
  • JS engine loaded from noyitz.github.io/flowstory/src/index.js
  • Diagram JSON embedded inline — nodes, tooltips, flows, and inspector mutations are all in one const diagram = {...} object
  • Auto-play with loop mode enabled on page load

The JSON schema declares:

  • Nodes with x, y, w, h coordinates, grouped inside boundary and container parent nodes
  • Tooltips keyed by node ID, with title, description, detail key-value pairs, and external links
  • Flows as ordered step arrays using arrow (animated edge) and lightup (node highlight) modes
  • Inspector mutations that update the right-panel request/response display at each step

Self-Contained

The entire diagram — 39 component tooltips, 38 flows with 632 steps, and full inspector mutations — lives in a single ~480KB HTML file with zero build tooling required. Just open it in a browser.

docs.title: Redfish BMC + Ironic Flow

The newest flow (Flow 13) shows the complete bare-metal onboarding path:

  1. Admin applies a BareMetalHost CR with a Redfish BMC address
  2. BMO (Bare Metal Operator) registers the node with Ironic
  3. Ironic Conductor calls Redfish REST endpoints on the BMC: GET /Systems/1, InsertMedia, Reset
  4. IPA (Ironic Python Agent) ramdisk boots, inspects hardware, reports inventory
  5. Ironic provisions RHEL 9 via IPA, reboots to HDD
  6. EDPM Ansible installs nova-compute, ovn-controller, libvirt
  7. Node registers with the control plane and starts accepting workloads

docs.title: Technical Blueprint and Curricular Syllabus for Mastering Red Hat OpenStack Services on OpenShift
docs.text:
Red Hat OpenStack Services on OpenShift (RHOSO) represents a fundamental shift in how enterprise Infrastructure-as-a-Service (IaaS) is designed, deployed, and managed. By migrating the traditional OpenStack control plane from legacy TripleO-directed bare-metal deployments into a podified, container-native architecture hosted on Red Hat OpenShift Container Platform (RHOCP), RHOSO delivers an efficient, declarative control plane while maintaining a highly performant, distributed data plane on bare-metal Red Hat Enterprise Linux (RHEL) nodes.

This paradigm shift requires platform administrators and systems engineers to develop new technical competencies. Mastering RHOSO demands proficiency across three foundational pillars—Compute, Networking, and Storage—alongside structured learning paths and advanced operational troubleshooting methodologies.

docs.title: Technical Mastery Domain 1: Compute Infrastructure
docs.text:
The compute tier in RHOSO shifts virtualization management from manual host-level scripting to a declarative framework driven by Kubernetes Custom Resource Definitions (CRDs). The platform uses the EDPM engine to execute containerized Ansible runners, enabling parallelized operations and establishing robust micro-failure domains across compute node sets.

+---------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
|                       COMPUTE NODE DECLARATIVE DEPLOYMENT                       |
|                                                                                 |
|   +-------------------------------------------------------------------------+   |
|   |                     OpenStackDataPlaneNodeSet CRD                       |   |
|   |   Defines structural parameters, SSH credentials, and role templates    |   |
|   +------------------------------------+------------------------------------+   |
|                                        |                                        |
|                                        v                                        |
|   +-------------------------------------------------------------------------+   |
|   |                       OpenStackDataPlaneService                         |   |
|   |  Determines the precise software stack and initialization configurations|   |
|   +------------------------------------+------------------------------------+   |
|                                        |                                        |
|                                        v                                        |
|   +-------------------------------------------------------------------------+   |
|   |                      Containerized Ansible Runner                       |   |
|   |     Deploys target configuration across RHEL hosts in parallel          |   |
|   +------------------------------------+------------------------------------+   |
|                                        |                                        |
|                                        v                                        |
|   +-------------------------------------------------------------------------+   |
|   |                     Initialized Compute Node Status                     |   |
|   |       Monitored continuously for drift and performance anomalies        |   |
|   +-------------------------------------------------------------------------+   |
+---------------------------------------------------------------------------------+

docs.title: Key Compute Core Concepts
docs.text:
To master compute orchestration within a podified cloud ecosystem, architects must gain competency in several core areas:

Declarative Machine Ingestion: Deploying compute nodes via declarative CRDs. This involves using the Bare Metal Operator (BMO) and configuring BareMetalHost and OpenStackDataPlaneNodeSet resources to automate OS installations and platform registration.

Image-Based Deployments: Preparing, customizing, and scaling target infrastructure nodes using containerized bootc (Image Mode) operating system images.

High Availability and Evacuation: Standardizing failure recovery using Instance High Availability (Instance HA) to automate the evacuation and recreation of virtual machines on healthy hosts when a physical compute failure is detected.

Distributed Edge Topologies: Implementing Distributed Compute Nodes (DCN) backed by local Red Hat Ceph Storage endpoints to support low-latency requirements.

Database and MQ Cell Architectures: Configuring and validating multi-cell environments to isolate database transactions and message queues, which mitigates scalability bottlenecks in large installations.

docs.text:
In RHOSO, networking transitions from legacy Neutron agents on bare-metal to an orchestrator-managed hierarchy. This design integrates the Kubernetes NMState operator for node network policies, Multus for multi-interface pods, and OVN-Kubernetes as the core SDN engine.

                |  into the control plane pods.                   |

+------------------+           +------------------+             +------------------+

|  Exposes service |           | Direct high-     |             |  Isolated VM-to- |
|  endpoints       |           | throughput path  |             |  VM data transit |

docs.title: Key Networking Core Concepts
docs.text:
Mastering this network virtualization topology requires addressing several integration challenges:

Host Network State Management: Writing declarative states via NMState to control interface bonds, VLAN interfaces, and MTU settings across OpenShift and data plane nodes.

Virtual IP Allocation and Announcement: Managing MetalLB configuration pools and Layer 2 or BGP announcements to ensure high availability for API service VIPs.

Dynamic Spine-Leaf Routing: Deploying dynamic routing on the data plane using Free Range Routing (FRR) and BGP, which requires Distributed Virtual Routing (DVR) to scale external traffic routing.

Load Balancing Resiliency: Configuring dynamic flow resumption in Octavia to automatically reassign active load-balancing tasks to surviving controllers during an outage.

Automated DNS Infrastructures: Deploying and managing Designate to provide multitenant, automated DNS-as-a-Service, integrated with the control plane's DNSmasq hierarchy and upstream enterprise DNS resolvers.

docs.title: Technical Mastery Domain 3: Storage Integration
docs.text:
The RHOSO storage framework manages two distinct storage pathways: persistent storage for control plane service states (e.g., databases) using Container Storage Interface (CSI) drivers, and scalable backends for virtual machines on the data plane.

|   |  - Targets transactional DB state  |  - Backed by Ceph, SAN, or NAS     |   |

|   |        LVM Container Volumes       |         Pure FA / Dell PowerFlex   |   |
|   +------------------------------------+------------------------------------+   |

docs.title: Key Storage Core Concepts
docs.text:
Mastering storage integration requires an understanding of persistent storage architectures:

Control Plane CSI Orchestration: Managing high-performance CSI storage engines like Portworx to handle persistent volumes for database and caching pods.

External Ceph Integration: Connecting Glance (image), Cinder (block), and Manila (file) services to external Red Hat Ceph Storage clusters.

Distributed Object Storage: Deploying Swift on external data plane nodes to improve horizontal scalability and performance for large object repositories.

Enterprise Multi-Backend Configuration: Integrating specialized drivers like the Pure Storage FlashArray volume driver or Dell PowerFlex SDC (Storage Data Client) to support multi-backend Cinder configurations.

Storage Bus Notifications: Enabling event notifications in Cinder and Manila by configuring notificationsBusInstance to output metrics to a RabbitMQ bus.

docs.title: Operational Troubleshooting and Diagnostic Blueprint
docs.text:
Diagnosing issues in a container-native, operator-driven control plane requires a structured troubleshooting methodology. Because failures can occur across container runtimes, Kubernetes operators, physical host nodes, or network configurations, administrators must systematically check components to identify the root cause.

  Control Plane / Podified Layer Diagnostics
                      |
                      v
     +----------------------------------+
     |   Verify OCP Operator Health     | <--- "oc get co" & "oc get clusterversion"
     +----------------+-----------------+
                      |
                      v
     +----------------------------------+
     | Inspect Pod Event Timelines      | <--- "oc get events -n openstack"
     +----------------+-----------------+
                      |
                      v
     +----------------------------------+
     | Validate Webhook Configuration   | <--- Check for webhook registration blockers
     +----------------------------------+
                      |
                      +---------------------------------------+
                      |                                       |
                      v                                       v
  Bare-Metal Host / NMState Diagnostics        EDPM Deployment Troubleshooting
                      |                                       |
                      v                                       v
     +----------------------------------+            +----------------------------------+
     |   Inspect NNCE Error Reports     |            | Run Specialized Diagnostic Tools |
     |   Check logs of NMState handler  |            | Execute "openstack-must-gather"  |
     +----------------------------------+            +----------------------------------+

docs.title: 1. Control Plane & Operator Diagnostics
docs.text:
When debugging control plane operators, administrators should first verify the overall health of the OpenShift operators and core cluster resources.

Operator Health Assessment: Run commands to check that the core operators are responding and healthy:

oc get co
oc get clusterversion

Pod Timeline Audit: Review the timeline of events within the openstack namespace to identify crashes, rescheduling loops, or provisioning delays:

oc get events -n openstack --sort-by=.lastTimestamp

Resource Pressure Evaluation: Check for memory or CPU contention on the host OpenShift nodes, which can cause pod eviction or database replication timeouts:

oc describe nodes | grep -E "CPU|Memory|Disk"
kubectl top node

docs.title: 2. Namespace Webhooks & Validation Constraints
docs.text:
A common issue during installation or upgrade is when custom resources fail to reconcile because API webhooks are blocked.

Namespace Validation: Verify that the target namespace is configured to allow privileged pod creation. If the Security Context Constraint (SCC) is set incorrectly, webhook execution will fail and prevent resource instantiation:

oc get namespace openstack -o jsonpath='{.metadata.labels}'

Namespace Label Configuration: Ensure the appropriate security context flags are applied to the namespace:

oc label ns openstack security.openshift.io/scc.podSecurityLabelSync=false --overwrite
oc label ns openstack pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce=privileged --overwrite

Custom Resource Name Verification: Ensure that custom resource definitions do not exceed the 63-character limit. Long names can trigger silent webhook validation errors or cause truncation issues during deployment.

docs.title: 3. NMState & Network Infrastructure Diagnostics
docs.text:
If host-level physical configurations are misconfigured, network isolation or interface routing can fail.

Network Policy Failures: When a NodeNetworkConfigurationPolicy (NNCP) fails to apply, check the generated NodeNetworkConfigurationEnactment (NNCE) objects for the target node to locate the configuration error:

oc get nnce -o yaml

Handler Log Extraction: Extract logs directly from the NMState handler daemon running on the failing physical host:

oc logs -n openshift-nmstate -l app=kubernetes-nmstate-handler --tail=100

ARP and Speaker Alignment Check: If MetalLB is failing to announce virtual VIP addresses, check if the Speaker pods are running on nodes that lack the physical OpenStack interfaces, which will prevent them from answering ARP queries.

docs.title: 4. EDPM & Data Plane Diagnostics
docs.text:
If a compute or networker node set fails to deploy or scale, administrators can use several diagnostics to isolate the issue.

Job Condition Verification: Inspect the validation status and message history of the failed job object within the targeted node set:

oc describe openstackdataplanenodeset <nodeset_name> -n openstack

Ansible Runner Log Analysis: Because EDPM runs via containerized Ansible environments, review the log stream of the active runner pod to identify the step where the execution failed:

oc logs -n openstack jobs/openstack-ansible-runner-<task-suffix>

Data Plane Target Verification: Check the SSH authorization configurations and verify that the target bare-metal hosts contain the private keys specified in the corresponding credential secret:

oc get secret dataplane-adoption-secret -n openstack -o jsonpath='{.data.ssh-privatekey}' | base64 -d

Comprehensive Data Gathering: Avoid generic OpenShift debugging commands. Instead, run the specialized OpenStack utility to capture full configuration states and logs across both the control and data planes:

oc adm must-gather --image=registry.redhat.io/rhoso/openstack-must-gather-rhel9:latest

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
RHOSO demands a cross-domain skill set spanning Kubernetes operators, declarative CRDs, bare-metal automation, and traditional OpenStack service expertise. The three mastery domains—Compute, Networking, and Storage—each have distinct architectural patterns but share a common operational model: define intent in YAML, reconcile via operators, and troubleshoot across both the podified control plane and the EDPM-managed data plane.

Use the structured curricula above as a progressive learning path: establish Linux and Ansible foundations, deepen OpenShift and OpenStack administration skills through official training, then specialize using the RHOSO 18.0 documentation for deployment customization, scale planning, and partner integrations.

docs.title: vLLM Architecture Deep Dive — From KV Cache Bottleneck to Production Inference
docs.text: Stepping into the production side of large language model deployment is an exciting milestone. To understand why vLLM (Versatile LLM) has become the gold standard for open-source model serving, we first need to examine the massive bottleneck it was built to solve: GPU memory. Every autoregressive generation step stores intermediate attention state in a KV cache — and how that cache is allocated determines whether your GPU serves ten concurrent users or a hundred.

docs.title: The Core Bottleneck: The KV Cache Problem
docs.text:
When a model generates text, it acts autoregressively — it predicts the next token based on all previous tokens. To avoid recomputing the mathematical context of past tokens at every single step, the system stores their Keys and Values in GPU memory. This is called the KV cache.

In traditional serving frameworks (like Hugging Face Transformers), memory for this KV cache had to be allocated contiguously and statically based on the maximum possible output length (e.g., 2048 or 4096 tokens).

docs.title: The Problem with Traditional Allocation
docs.text:
• Internal fragmentation: If a user only requests a 10-token answer but the system reserved space for 2048 tokens, the remaining 2038 slots sit completely empty and locked up.
  • External fragmentation: Memory gets broken into tiny scattered gaps that can't be reused for new requests.
  • Because of this, up to 60% to 80% of a GPU's VRAM used to be entirely wasted, severely limiting how many concurrent users a server could handle.

The real cost of wasted VRAM

Naive pre-allocation reserves max_len tokens per sequence regardless of actual output length. With PagedAttention, memory waste drops below 4%, enabling 2–4× more concurrent sequences on the same hardware.

docs.title: The Two Pillars of vLLM Architecture
docs.text: vLLM addresses the KV cache problem through two tightly coupled innovations:

docs.title: 1. PagedAttention
docs.text: Inspired by how operating systems use virtual memory and paging to manage RAM, vLLM treats GPU VRAM as a pool of individual, fixed-size blocks (typically 16 tokens per block). A block table keeps track of which logical sequence tokens map to which physical memory blocks — non-contiguous, dynamically allocated, with copy-on-write support for parallel sampling.

docs.title: 2. Continuous Batching (Iteration-Level Scheduling)
docs.text: Traditional batching forces the server to wait until every single request in a batch is completely finished. vLLM uses continuous batching at the iteration level (token-by-token). As soon as a single request completes, its memory is instantly freed, and a new request jumps into the active batch on the very next cycle.

docs.title: Scheduler — The Brain
docs.text:
The scheduler decides which requests get processed in each iteration and in what order. It implements:

  • Continuous batching — doesn't wait for an entire batch to finish before admitting new requests
  • Preemption policies — when GPU memory is exhausted, it can swap KV cache blocks to CPU or recompute them later
  • Priority queues — manages waiting, running, and swapped request queues

Each scheduling iteration produces a SchedulerOutput containing prefill and decode assignments for the current batch — often a mixed batch of sequences at different lifecycle stages.

docs.title: Block Manager — PagedAttention's Memory Layer
docs.text:
The block manager implements a paging system inspired by OS virtual memory:

Concept OS Analogy vLLM Implementation Page 4 KB memory page KV cache block (e.g., 16 tokens worth of K and V tensors) Page table Virtual → physical mapping Block table mapping logical block index → physical GPU block Swap space Disk swap CPU memory for evicted blocks

Key properties:

  • Non-contiguous memory — blocks can live anywhere in the physical pool
  • Copy-on-write — enables efficient parallel sampling (multiple outputs from one prompt)
  • Dynamic allocation — blocks are allocated only as tokens are generated

docs.title: Model Executor & Workers
docs.text:
• One Worker per GPU (for tensor parallelism)
  • Each worker holds a shard of the model weights
  • Workers execute the forward pass in lockstep using NCCL for all-reduce operations

docs.title: Attention Backend
docs.text:
vLLM selects optimized kernels depending on the phase:

Phase Kernel Why Prefill FlashAttention Parallel processing of long prompts Decode PagedAttention Scattered KV blocks via block table lookup Alternative FlashInfer Drop-in backend for certain hardware/configs

docs.title: The Full Inference Pipeline
docs.text:
Here is the complete path from request arrival to streamed response:

sequenceDiagram
    participant Client
    participant API as API Server
    participant Engine as LLM Engine
    participant Sched as Scheduler
    participant BM as Block Manager
    participant GPU as Model Runner

    Client->>API: POST /v1/chat/completions
    API->>Engine: Create SequenceGroup
    Engine->>Engine: Tokenize prompt
    Engine->>Sched: Enqueue sequence
    Sched->>BM: Check free blocks
    BM-->>Sched: Blocks available
    Sched->>GPU: Prefill batch
    GPU->>BM: Store KV in blocks
    loop Decode (token-by-token)
        Sched->>GPU: Decode batch (mixed prefill + decode)
        GPU->>BM: Read/write KV blocks
        GPU->>GPU: Sample next token
        GPU-->>API: Stream token
        API-->>Client: SSE chunk
    end
    Sched->>BM: Release blocks
    API-->>Client: [DONE]

docs.title: Step 1: Request Arrival
docs.text: The API server (FastAPI) receives an HTTP request and creates a SequenceGroup — the unit of work that tracks one or more related generation sequences (e.g., n=3 parallel samples).

docs.title: Step 2: Tokenization
docs.text: The input text is tokenized into token IDs. For chat models, the prompt is formatted according to the model's chat template before tokenization.

docs.title: Step 3: Scheduling Decision
docs.text: The scheduler checks available blocks in the block manager. If memory permits, the sequence is admitted to the running queue. The scheduler produces a SchedulerOutput with prefill and/or decode assignments for this iteration.

docs.title: Step 4: Prefill Phase
docs.text:
All prompt tokens are processed in parallel in a single (or chunked) forward pass. Attention computes K and V tensors for every prompt token, which are stored in newly allocated KV cache blocks. This is the most compute-intensive phase for long prompts.

Chunked prefill

For very long prompts, vLLM can split prefill into chunks and interleave them with ongoing decode work — reducing latency spikes for other requests in the batch.

docs.title: Step 5: Decode Phase
docs.text:
Generation proceeds token by token. Each iteration:

  1. The PagedAttention kernel reads scattered KV blocks via the block table
  2. The model computes logits for the next token
  3. A new K/V pair is appended (allocating a new block when the current 16-token block fills)

docs.title: Step 6: Continuous Batching
docs.text:
On every iteration, the scheduler assembles a fresh batch. Completed sequences drop out immediately; new sequences (prefill) or continuing sequences (decode) take their place. A single batch may contain:

  • Sequences in prefill (processing prompts)
  • Sequences in decode (generating one token each)

This is what makes GPU utilization stay high under variable load.

docs.title: Step 7: Sampling
docs.text:
Raw logits pass through the sampling pipeline:

logits → temperature scaling → top-p (nucleus) → top-k → softmax → sample

The chosen token ID becomes the next input for the decode loop.

docs.title: Step 8: Stopping Conditions
docs.text:
Generation stops when any of these conditions is met:

  • EOS token — end-of-sequence marker emitted by the model
  • max_tokens — user-specified output limit reached
  • Stop sequences — custom strings configured by the caller

docs.title: Step 9: Detokenization & Streaming
docs.text: Token IDs are converted back to text. Partial results are streamed to the client via Server-Sent Events (SSE), giving users low time-to-first-token and incremental output.

docs.title: Step 10: Completion and Cleanup
docs.text: When a sequence finishes, its KV cache blocks are returned to the free pool and immediately available for new requests — the core benefit of dynamic, non-contiguous allocation.

docs.title: PagedAttention: Memory Before and After
docs.text:
Without PagedAttention (naive allocation):

  • Pre-allocate max_len for each sequence regardless of actual length
  • 60–80% of KV cache memory wasted
  • Severe fragmentation limits concurrency

With PagedAttention:

  • Blocks scattered in physical memory; block table maps logical → physical
  • Memory waste drops to < 4%
  • 2–4× more concurrent sequences on the same GPU

docs.title: Traditional vs. vLLM Serving
docs.text: Feature Traditional Serving vLLM Serving KV cache allocation Statically allocated, continuous chunks Dynamically allocated, non-contiguous pages VRAM utilization Low (~20–40% used effectively) High (~96%+ used effectively) Batching style Static / dynamic (request-level) Continuous (iteration / token-level) Scalability Struggles heavily under high concurrency Scales horizontally across multiple GPUs smoothly Memory fragmentation High (internal + external) Minimal (< 4% waste) Latency under load Queues grow; GPU sits idle between batches Mixed prefill/decode keeps GPU busy

docs.title: Multi-GPU: Tensor Parallelism
docs.text:
When a model exceeds single-GPU memory, vLLM splits weights across devices using tensor parallelism:

  • Model weights are split column-wise across GPUs
  • Each GPU holds a shard of both model weights and KV cache blocks
  • After attention and FFN layers, NCCL all-reduce synchronizes partial results
  • One Worker per GPU executes forward passes in lockstep
vllm serve meta-llama/Llama-3.1-70B-Instruct \
  --tensor-parallel-size 4 \
  --dtype auto \
  --gpu-memory-utilization 0.9

This is distinct from pipeline parallelism (layer splitting) and data parallelism (replicated weights, sharded batches) — vLLM's primary multi-GPU strategy for large models is tensor parallelism.

docs.title: Advanced Performance Techniques
docs.text:
Beyond PagedAttention and continuous batching, vLLM implements a suite of optimizations for production workloads:

Technique What it solves PagedAttention Memory fragmentation → more concurrent sequences Continuous batching GPU idle time → higher throughput FlashAttention (prefill) Slow attention on long prompts Chunked prefill Latency spikes when long prompts monopolize the GPU Tensor parallelism Model doesn't fit on one GPU Quantization (AWQ / GPTQ / FP8) Reduce memory footprint + increase throughput Speculative decoding Decode latency — a small draft model predicts ahead, verified by the main model Prefix caching Redundant prefill for shared system prompts across requests

Speculative decoding in brief

A lightweight draft model generates several candidate tokens ahead of time. The main model verifies them in a single forward pass. Accepted tokens skip individual decode iterations, reducing latency for memory-bandwidth-bound workloads.

Prefix caching in brief

When multiple requests share an identical prefix (common with system prompts or RAG context), vLLM caches the KV blocks for that prefix. Subsequent requests with the same prefix skip the prefill computation entirely.

docs.title: Putting It Together
docs.text:
vLLM's design follows a clear principle: treat GPU memory like an OS treats RAM. Fixed-size pages, dynamic allocation, eviction to swap, and iteration-level scheduling together transform LLM serving from a memory-bound afterthought into a throughput engine.

The inference loop — tokenize, schedule, prefill, decode, sample, stream — runs continuously. Blocks are allocated on demand, freed on completion, and immediately reused. Attention kernels switch between FlashAttention (parallel prefill) and PagedAttention (scattered decode). Under load, mixed batches keep the GPU saturated while new requests flow in without waiting for batch boundaries.
